q: Your friend Acestes is of Trojan kind;

s: Acestes ascends the throne (as the new king)
q: And the new king ascends the throne with joy;

s: Acesta is named after Acestes’ name (common town)
q: Here you may build a common town for all, And, from Acestes’ name, Acesta call.

s: founding of Acesta is designed by the prince (with the plow)
q: The prince designs a city with the plow; The lots their sev’ral tenements allow.

s: Anchises is honored as a god
q: Anchises, last, is honour’d as a god;

s: Anchises appears to Aeneas (as a shade in a nocturnal vision)
q: ’Twas dead of night; when to his slumb’ring eyes His father’s shade descended from the skies,

s: Anchises dwells in Elysian plains (among the blessed dead)
q: But breathes the living air of soft Elysian plains.

s: Aeneas’s followers include the chosen youth (those who nobly dare)
q: The chosen youth, and those who nobly dare, Transport, to tempt the dangers of the war.

s: Venus is a mother goddess (protective of Aeneas)
q: Meantime the mother goddess, full of fears,

s: Venus is mother of Aeneas (protective mother)
q: For what remains, your godhead I implore, And trust my son to your protecting pow’r.

s: Neptune is a ruler of the sea (protector of Aeneas’s fleet)
q: Then thus the mighty Ruler of the Main:

s: Neptune’s protection protects Aeneas’s voyage (securing the fleet’s passage to Latium)
q: My will’s the same: fair goddess, fear no more, Your fleet shall safely gain the Latian shore;

s: Neptune protects Trojan fleet (by calming the sea and ensuring safe passage)
q: On Neptune’s faith the floating fleet relies; But what the man forsook, the god supplies, And o’er the dang’rous deep secure the navy flies;

s: Sleep is a god (soft and dream-bearing)
q: When the soft God of Sleep, with easy flight, Descends, and draws behind a trail of light.

s: Sleep makes prey of Palinurus
q: Thou, Palinurus, art his destin’d prey;

s: Palinurus is a master pilot (chief navigator of the fleet)
q: Ahead of all the master pilot steers;

s: Palinurus is plunged into the sea (by the god)
q: The god, insulting with superior strength, Fell heavy on him, plung’d him in the sea, And, with the stern, the rudder tore away.

s: Juno sends Iris (to pursue revenge)
q: And sends the goddess of the various bow, To try new methods of revenge below;

s: Iris is a goddess (goddess of the rainbow)
q: And sends the goddess of the various bow,

s: Fortune resumes her ancient hate
q: But Fortune soon resum’d her ancient hate;

s: Beroe is a woman (venerable aged dame)
q: In face and shape old Beroe she became, Doryclus’ wife, a venerable dame, Once blest with riches, and a mother’s name.

s: Aeneas is a Trojan prince
q: The pious prince ascends the sacred hill

s: Sibyl of Cumae is named Deiphobe
q: The priestess of the god, Deiphobe her name.

s: Deiphobe dwells in the Sibyl’s cave (deep within the cave)
q: Deep in a cave the Sibyl makes abode

s: Deiphobe is a priestess of Proserpine (of the nightly underworld)
q: nor Proserpine in vain Has made you priestess of her nightly reign

s: Apollo inspires Sibyl of Cumae (by possessing her organs and soul)
q: Commands his entrance, and, without control, Usurps her organs and inspires her soul

s: Apollo is a god (whose oracle speaks through the Sibyl)
q: When all the god came rushing on her soul.

s: Anchises is father of Aeneas
q: O goddess-born of great Anchises’ line

s: Anchises is deceased dead (before Aeneas’s descent)
q: Oft, since he breath’d his last, in dead of night His reverend image stood before my sight

s: Aeneas is a goddess-born hero
q: O goddess-born of great Anchises’ line

s: Proserpine owns the golden bough (as queen of the underworld)
q: There stands a tree; the queen of Stygian Jove Claims it her own

s: Proserpine receives the golden bough (as a required offering)
q: This from the vulgar branches must be torn, And to fair Proserpine the present borne

s: Misenus is a warrior (renowned for trumpet playing)
q: Son of the God of Winds: none so renown’d The warrior trumpet in the field to sound

s: Misenus serves Hector (with trumpet and spear)
q: He serv’d great Hector, and was ever near, Not with his trumpet only, but his spear

s: Misenus serves Aeneas (after Hector’s death)
q: But by Pelides’ arms when Hector fell, He chose Aeneas; and he chose as well

s: Misenus is killed by Triton (after provoking the sea gods)
q: Swoln with applause, and aiming still at more, He now provokes the sea gods from the shore; With envy Triton heard the martial sound, And the bold champion, for his challenge, drown’d

s: the Trojans perform Misenus’s funeral (with lamentation and sacrificial rites)
q: Meantime the Trojan troops, with weeping eyes, To dead Misenus pay his obsequies

s: the Trojans build the funeral pyre (for Misenus)
q: First, from the ground a lofty pile they rear, Of pitch trees, oaks, and pines, and unctuous fir

s: Aeneas is son of Anchises
q: O goddess-born of great Anchises’ line

s: Cumae contains Cumaean temple (dedicated to Apollo)
q: And here alighting, built this costly frame. Inscrib’d to Phoebus

s: Cumaean temple is dedicated to Apollo
q: And here alighting, built this costly frame. Inscrib’d to Phoebus

s: the Sibyl’s cave contains a hundred doors (with a hundred entrances and echoes)
q: A spacious cave, within its farmost part, Was hew’d and fashion’d by laborious art Thro’ the hill’s hollow sides: before the place, A hundred doors a hundred entries grace

s: the Underworld is surrounded by Cocytus (with black waters)
q: th’ infernal bounds Cocytus, with his sable waves, surrounds

s: Acheron is a innavigable river (surrounding the dark abode)
q: the dark abode Which Acheron surrounds, th’ innavigable flood

s: Lake Avernus is a lake (deadly and without light)
q: And there th’ unnavigable lake extends, O’er whose unhappy waters, void of light

s: Lake Avernus has deadly stenches (rising from its depths)
q: Such deadly stenches from the depths arise, And steaming sulphur, that infects the skies

s: the golden bough is a sacred branch (with radiant gold leaves and rind)
q: One bough it bears; but wondrous to behold! The ductile rind and leaves of radiant gold

s: Aeneas leads the Trojans (during the quest for Italy)
q: Thus far, by fate’s decrees and thy commands, Thro’ ambient seas and thro’ devouring sands, Our exil’d crew has sought th’ Ausonian ground

s: the funeral pyre contains Misenus’s body (during the cremation rites)
q: Then on a bier, with purple cover’d o’er, The breathless body, thus bewail’d, they lay, And fire the pile

s: the offerings and sacrifices honor Misenus (during his funeral rites)
q: Pure oil and incense on the fire they throw, And fat of victims, which his friends bestow

s: the Trojan-Italian wars include Tiber (running with blood)
q: Wars, horrid wars, I view; a field of blood, And Tiber rolling with a purple flood

s: Aeneas seeks Anchises (among the dead)
q: Conduct me thro’ the regions void of light, And lead me longing to my father’s sight

s: Aeneas carries the golden bough (as an offering to Proserpine)
q: He seiz’d the shining bough with griping hold, And rent away, with ease, the ling’ring gold; Then to the Sibyl’s palace bore the prize

s: Aeneas performs Misenus’s funeral (with the Trojans)
q: All weep; but most Aeneas mourns his fate, And hastens to perform the funeral state

s: Aeneas descends into the Underworld (guided by the Sibyl)
q: These rites perform’d, the prince, without delay, Hastes to the nether world his destin’d way

s: Sibyl of Cumae is a priestess (of Apollo)
q: And by his side the mad divining dame, The priestess of the god, Deiphobe her name

s: Aeneas is a Trojan chief
q: The Trojan chief, whose lineage is from Jove, Much fam’d for arms, and more for filial love,

s: Aeneas meets Dido (in the Mournful Fields)
q: Not far from these Phoenician Dido stood,

s: Aeneas meets Deiphobus (in the warrior souls’ region)
q: Here Priam’s son, Deiphobus, he found,

s: Aeneas fixes the golden bough (on Pluto’s palace door)
q: He fix’d the fatal bough requir’d by Pluto’s love.

s: Sibyl of Cumae is a prophetess
q: Scarce had he said, the prophetess began:

s: Sibyl of Cumae explains the Underworld (to Aeneas)
q: The Sibyl said, “you see the Stygian floods, The sacred stream which heav’n’s imperial state Attests in oaths, and fears to violate.

s: Sibyl of Cumae carries the golden bough (concealed in her clothing)
q: Then shew’d the shining bough, conceal’d within her vest.

s: Sibyl of Cumae prepares a sop (for Cerberus)
q: The prudent Sibyl had before prepar’d A sop, in honey steep’d, to charm the guard;

s: Anchises is a Aeneas's dead sire
q: Or, if by dearer ties you may be won, By your dead sire, and by your living son,

s: Aeneas is a living mortal (during the journey)
q: Mortal, whate’er, who this forbidden path In arms presum’st to tread, I charge thee, stand,

s: Anchises resides in Elysium (as a shade)
q: Is sent to seek his sire in your Elysian grove.

s: the gods rule the regions of the night
q: Ye gods who rule the regions of the night,

s: the gods command Aeneas (through fate and divine authority)
q: Unwilling I forsook your friendly state, Commanded by the gods, and forc’d by fate.

s: the ghosts are forms without bodies (in the Underworld)
q: Forms without bodies, and impassive air.

s: the ghosts are ferried by Charon (when buried)
q: The boatman, Charon; those, the buried host, He ferries over to the farther coast;

s: the Underworld contains the Mournful Fields (as a region of lovers)
q: Not far from thence, the Mournful Fields appear So call’d from lovers that inhabit there.

s: the Underworld contains Tartarus (as the region of punishment)
q: The left to that unhappy region tends, Which to the depth of Tartarus descends;

s: Hell contains the infernal monsters (near its gate)
q: Of various forms unnumber’d spectres more, Centaurs, and double shapes, besiege the door.

s: Aeneas is descended from Jupiter
q: The Trojan chief, whose lineage is from Jove,

s: Acheron flows into Cocytus (through troubled eddies)
q: Whose troubled eddies, thick with ooze and clay, Are whirl’d aloft, and in Cocytus lost.

s: Styx is a sacred stream (binding the gods by oath)
q: The sacred stream which heav’n’s imperial state Attests in oaths, and fears to violate.

s: Elysium is a grove (where Anchises resides)
q: Is sent to seek his sire in your Elysian grove.

s: the buried dead are ferried across Styx (by Charon)
q: The boatman, Charon; those, the buried host, He ferries over to the farther coast;

s: the unburied dead wander the shore (for a hundred years)
q: A hundred years they wander on the shore; At length, their penance done, are wafted o’er.”

s: the unburied dead are denied funeral rites (until their penance is complete)
q: The ghosts rejected are th’ unhappy crew Depriv’d of sepulchers and fun’ral due:

s: Charon rules the dreary coast
q: There Charon stands, who rules the dreary coast:

s: Charon rules the dreary coast
q: There Charon stands, who rules the dreary coast:
